1.pericope_label: The people gather at the water gate; Ezra reads the law from the wooden pulpit, and the Levites give the sense so that the people understand

schools.summary: Gill calls the street large and commodious and the people unanimous, zealous and affectionate, thinks Ezra read selected passages rather than straight through, reports the Hebrew word for the pulpit as a tower named for its height, form and size since it held fourteen men, and makes the opening blessing a short wholly benedictory prayer offered so that what followed might carry greater authority.

Henry dates the assembly to the feast of trumpets and adds why the day carried extra weight, the altar having been set up on it after the return within living memory; he holds that while sacrifice was tied to the temple door, prayer and praise and preaching are as acceptable in one place as another.

Clarke makes it the first day of the civil year, places the water gate on the road to the brook Kidron, excludes those incapable of instruction without shutting out a mother with a crying child, calls the platform the first intimation we have of a pulpit, and builds the fullest case on the eighth verse, that the loss of Hebrew in Babylon produced both the Chaldee paraphrases and probably preaching from a text, analysed in four steps. Wesley has the Levites translate into the Chaldee the people now spoke and then expound and apply the meaning.

Ellicott finds the unanimity rather than the number emphatic, notes that Ezra appears here for the first time in the book after probably twelve years at court, has the readers choosing passages hour after hour from daylight, describes the double Amen with lifted hands and the faces bowed, and points out that the great God is the historian phrase and not the reader own. Delitzsch places six men on the right and seven on the left and argues a name has dropped from the Hebrew, and dissents on the disputed word of the eighth verse.

debates.question: What does it mean that they read distinctly and gave the sense?

sides.position: they rendered the Hebrew into the Chaldee the people now spoke, and then expounded and applied the meaning
they expounded the obscurer passages, naturally turning them into the vernacular

the loss of the ancient language made translation necessary, and the practice was the origin of the Chaldee paraphrases and probably of preaching from a text; reading distinctly means expanding the import of every word, giving the sense means showing the hearers how nearly it concerned them

the sense the Rabbis give it, a rendering into the vulgar tongue, cannot be shown to belong to the word, nor will a distinct recitation by appointed rules do; what is meant is a paraphrastic exposition and application of the law

debates.question: What was the pulpit, and who stood on it?

sides.position: a tower of wood large enough for fourteen men, the name still borne by synagogue pulpits
a raised platform so that the people could see and hear, and the first intimation we have of a pulpit
a stage built for the purpose with six on the right and seven on the left, a name having dropped from the Hebrew text

debates.question: Why did this day carry such weight?

sides.position: it was the feast of trumpets, and the day the altar had been set up after the return, still within living memory
the seventh was the most important month and its first day the most important new moon
it was the first day of the civil year, ushered in by the sound of trumpets

outliers: Clarke alone refuses to let the pulpit be imagined like the tubs set up in churches, where a preacher is nearly as confined as in the stocks.
Ellicott alone points out that the great God is the historian own phrase, the words Ezra used not being reported.
Clarke alone will not have a mother shut out of the assembly because her child cries.
themes: a congregation that asked to be read to
a tower built for a reader
a language lost and a sense supplied
the day preaching from a text may have begun

9.pericope_label: The people weep at the words of the law, and are told that the day is holy and the joy of the LORD is their strength

schools.summary: Gill glosses the Tirshatha as governor, the post Zerubbabel had held, and closes the scene plainly, the Levites making the people quiet and easy with the governor behind them and the people going their way to eat and drink freely and cheerfully.

Henry accounts for the weeping by what the law does, working death and speaking terror and thundering a curse, takes the wound for a good sign of tender hearts like Josiah, notes that when some wept all wept since each saw himself guilty, observes that Nehemiah enters the chapter only here, and lays down that sorrow for sin must not hinder joy in God but lead to it.

Clarke settles that the Tirshatha is Nehemiah by office, reads the command as eating and drinking the best they have while remembering those who cannot feast, and denies that this is a gluttonous festival that enervates body and mind, holding instead that religious joy tempered by dependence, meekness and self-diffidence strengthens the soul until every duty is practicable and delightful. Wesley adds that cheerful and thankful service will give the strength of mind and body needed to perform their duties and to oppose their enemies designs.

Ellicott explains the prohibition of mourning from the calendar, the days of high festival being unsuitable for public sorrow with the Day of Atonement and a day of fasting and covenant still to come, renders the famous clause literally as delight in Jehovah being a strong refuge, and marks the almost irrepressible emotion the Levites had to quiet. Delitzsch identifies what was read as sections of Deuteronomy and other parts of the law chosen to convict the people of transgression.

sides.position: because the law works death and speaks terror, showing men their sin and danger, and their hearts were tender enough to feel it
because what was read were sections chosen to convict them of transgressing the commandments and of the punishments they had incurred
the day was holy and to be kept with joy and praise, and sorrow for sin must lead to joy in God rather than hinder it
days of high festival were unsuitable for public sorrow, and the Day of Atonement and a day of fasting and covenant were already coming
the day was appointed for rejoicing in him who had turned their captivity and restored the law

debates.question: In what sense is the joy of the LORD their strength?

sides.position: literally, delight in Jehovah is a strong refuge, a sentence capable of unlimited application
a religious feast strengthens body and mind, and joy tempered by dependence and meekness makes every duty practicable and delightful
cheerful and thankful service gives the strength needed both to perform their duties and to oppose their enemies

outliers: Clarke alone ends on the proverb that a cheerful heart is not only a continual feast but a continual medicine.
Henry alone notices that Nehemiah is brought into the chapter at this verse and not before.
Clarke alone presses the second half of the command, that the joy be made general by sending portions to those who cannot feast.
themes: a law that wounds before it heals
mourning ruled out by the calendar
a feast that must reach the poor to be kept

13.pericope_label: On the second day the heads of the people study the law, find the feast of tabernacles written, and keep it with booths and daily reading

schools.summary: Gill dates the second gathering to the day after the trumpets and the reading, has the people find the command either from that reading or in conversation with Ezra, sends them out to the mountains near the city for branches, keeps the feast at Jerusalem only, and confirms the daily reading where before only the first and last days had been convocations.

Henry makes the second day gathering the proof of the first day work, the chief returning on a day that was no festival because they found it more gainful than any worldly pleasure, and notes the reversal of places: on the first day Ezra humility set the priests and Levites at his right hand and his left as fellow teachers, on the second their own humility set them at his feet as learners.

Clarke recalls what the feast commemorated and why men just out of Babylon owed it the more, reminds the reader that eastern houses have flat roofs used for rest and sleep, says that no celebration since Joshua had been so hearty or so pious, and dismisses the legend of the hidden sacred fire as worthy of no credit. Wesley credits the Levites with confessing ignorance rather than pretending to knowledge, identifies the mount of Olives and why its trees stood there, and distinguishes the two ways this keeping surpassed every other.

Ellicott notes that only the chief of the fathers came while the great feast was still to come, that the festival was almost forgotten and the booths disused, that no such command as the proclamation stands in the law so that an emendation is preferable, and that the branches gathered were such as circumstances allowed rather than those the ancient law named; he hears the pathos in the title children of the captivity. Delitzsch leaves the reader of the law indefinite and sets two limits, that the reading was required only in a sabbatical year and that the last day meant is the seventh.

debates.question: Where does the proclamation about branches come from?

sides.position: no such command stands in the law; the Greek inserts a clause naming Ezra, but an emendation giving when they heard it they proclaimed is better, and the branches are such as circumstances allowed
the mount is the mount of Olives, whose trees were planted thereabouts chiefly for the city use at this very feast
for everything concerning this feast the reader is referred to the law itself

debates.question: In what sense had the feast not been kept so since Joshua?

sides.position: it had been kept before, but never thus, with the whole people dwelling in booths
never so joyfully, having new causes of rejoicing added to the old, and never so religiously, the law being read on every day instead of the first and last only
no celebration since the days of Joshua had been so heartily or so piously performed

debates.question: Who read the law daily, and under what rule?

sides.position: Ezra read it every day of the feast
the subject is indefinite, though others supply Ezra; the law required this reading only at the tabernacles of a sabbatical year, and the last day meant is the seventh

outliers: Clarke alone dismisses the legend of the sacred fire hidden in a dry well and rekindled by a break of sunlight.
Henry alone marks the reversal by which the teachers of the first day became the learners of the second.
Ellicott alone distinguishes the booths the temple ministers made from those strangers put up in the streets and open spaces by the gates.
themes: teachers who sat down as learners
a festival recovered from the text
a week of reading where two days had served
